newsitem.title: MEXICO: OECD sees Latam growth picking up in 1997.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees Latam growth picking up in 1997.

text.p: Economic growth is likely to pick up in Central and South America next year but excessive government spending could torpedo the recovery, the OECD said on Thursday.

"Assuming continued budget discipline, output growth will probably accelerate gradually over the coming year or so, reaching more than four percent in 1998," the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said in its twice-yearly economic outlook.
Average growth in Central and South America was just 2.1 percent in 1995. But it will rise to 2.7 percent this year and 3.8 percent in 1997, the organisation forecast.

The OECD said the recovery would be jeopardised if governments used higher tax revenues to loosen controls on spending. This would hurt confidence, push up interest rates and create a "vicious circle of recession and capital flight".
Assuming governments did not lose budget discipline, inflation would come down across the region but trade deficits were likely to worsen, the organisation said.

Latin American countries would be able to handle the larger trade gaps if they relied less on foreign money to finance their economies and ensured that investment from abroad was committed for the longer term, the report said.

Because of its size Brazil remained one of the keys to Latin American economic stability, the OECD said. Brazil's fiscal improvement was expected to accelerate next year as privatisation and tax revenues grew and payroll costs were held steady.

Elsewhere in the region, Argentina's budget deficit was likely to fall if its parliament approved a fiscal package now under discussion, the report said. It called for tighter government control on spending in Colombia but said neighbouring Venezuela would benefit greatly from higher oil prices.
